meanings.note: Invariable modal word: introduces polite requests (ممكن أعرف؟ 'may I know?', ممكن تضبي... 'could you...') and possibility (ممكن تخسر 'might lose').

examples.trans: May I ask you a question?
Anything could happen.

meanings.note: Everyday Levantine verb for packing things up; تضبي لسانك literally tells someone to pack their tongue away.

examples.trans: I packed my books into my bag.
Pack your things before we leave.

meanings.note: Used in idioms about speaking or keeping quiet (تضبي لسانك).

examples.trans: She has a sharp tongue when replying.
Hold your tongue in front of them.

meanings.note: Everyday Levantine word for 'inside' (جوا حلقك 'inside your mouth/throat').

examples.trans: The girls are sitting inside the classroom.
Keep the book inside the bag.

meanings.note: Appears in the vivid Jordanian idiom ضبي لسانك جوا حلقك ('tuck your tongue inside your throat' = keep quiet).

examples.trans: My throat hurt from talking.
Keep your tongue inside your mouth for a bit.

meanings.note: Softens adjectives, requests, and verbs (صعبة شوي، ارتحت شوي).

examples.trans: Wait for me a bit by the door.
The test was a little hard.

meanings.note: Past tense linking verb (كنت، كنتي، كان، كنا) and subjunctive تكون / نكون ('to be'); ما كان عندي means 'I didn't have'.

examples.trans: I was at school in the morning.
Today was very long.

meanings.note: Standard Levantine future marker placed before a bare subjunctive verb (رح أخلص، ما رح نسكت).

examples.trans: I'm going to tell the truth.
I won't forget this day.

meanings.note: Used when someone nearly blows a secret in public (كنتي رح تفضحينا 'you were going to expose us').

examples.trans: Lower your voice, don't give us away!
Her look gave everything away.

meanings.note: Everyday Levantine preposition taking nouns (قدام المديرة) or suffixes (قدامهم 'in front of them').

examples.trans: She stood in front of the whole class.
Act normal in front of them.

meanings.note: Singular بنت, definite البنت, plural بنات / البنات ('AlRawabi School for Girls' = مدرسة الروابي للبنات).

examples.trans: She is a very bright girl.
The girls are standing in the courtyard.

meanings.note: Everyday oath used earnestly to swear one is telling the truth (والله ما حكيت إشي) or surprisedly in والله جد؟ ('oh really?').

examples.trans: I swear I'm telling the truth.
Honestly, I'm glad to see you.

meanings.note: Negates past and b-present verbs (ما إجيت، ما بعرف) and idioms like ما عليكم ('never mind'); after قبل or بدل (قبل ما، بدل ما) it links a verb clause.

examples.trans: I didn't hear the bell.
Come before the school closes.

meanings.note: The main Levantine verb for 'talk / say / tell', far more common in Amman than تكلم.

examples.trans: Who told you the news?
Tell me what happened with you.

meanings.note: Signature Jordanian/Palestinian word corresponding to formal شيء; definite form الإشي, plural أشياء.

examples.trans: There is something important I want to say.
Nothing happened.

meanings.note: Placed before a name or title whenever addressing someone directly (يا دينا، يا مس فاتن); natural English usually drops it.

examples.trans: Come here, Mariam.
Thank you very much, Miss.

meanings.note: Core Levantine question word for 'what?' (شو صار؟) and casual conversation starter ('So, ...').

examples.trans: What are you doing here?
So, ready to go?

meanings.note: With pronoun suffixes: ما كان قصدي ('I didn't mean to') and شو قصدك؟ ('what do you mean?').

examples.trans: I swear I didn't mean to upset you.
What do you mean by this question?

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine demonstrative used before a definite noun (هاد الإشي، هاد الحكي) or as a pronoun (حتى لو هاد آخر إشي).

examples.trans: Is this book yours?
This isn't fair at all.

meanings.note: Verbal noun of حكى; هاد الحكي means 'this talk / this claim'.

examples.trans: This talk is unacceptable.
I heard all the talk that happened.

meanings.note: High-frequency Levantine word for 'now' (contracted from هاد الوقت).

examples.trans: We have to go to class right now.
I feel a bit relieved now.

meanings.note: Appears in المرة الجاي ('next time'), أول وآخر مرة ('first and last time'), بالمرة ('at all'), and plural مرات ('sometimes').

examples.trans: This is the first time I come here.
Sometimes we sit in the library.

meanings.note: Negates nouns, adjectives, participles, prepositional phrases, and لازم (مش صح، مش معنا، مش قادرة، مش بعد اليوم).

examples.trans: This talk is not true.
I'm not upset with you.

meanings.note: Versatile noun: ما عندي وقت ('no time'), صار الوقت ('it's time'), وقتها ('at that moment / then'), مش وقته ('not the time for it').

examples.trans: I didn't have time to explain.
Everything is nice in its own time.

meanings.note: Invariable modal word followed by a subjunctive verb (لازم نتحمل، مش لازم نلفت نظرهم).

examples.trans: We have to go to class now.
We mustn't talk loudly.

meanings.note: Pairs with انتباه ('catch attention': لفت انتباهي) or نظر ('draw eyes': نلفت نظرهم).

examples.trans: Her words caught the principal's attention.
We don't want to draw anyone's attention.

meanings.note: In نلفت نظرهم ('draw their eyes/attention'), pairs with لفت.

examples.trans: We don't want to catch the teacher's eye.
Your point of view is clear.

meanings.note: Spoken Levantine dative base taking pronoun endings: إلي (to me), إلك (to you), إلها (to her), إلنا (for us), إلهم (to them).

examples.trans: This book is for you.
Tell me the truth.

meanings.note: With demonstrative هـ + الـ, هالفترة means 'during this period / right now'.

examples.trans: I'm very busy these days.
A hard period passed over us.

meanings.note: Spelled في in casual Levantine writing and negated directly with ما (ما في مكان 'there is no place', ما في حدا 'nobody is here').

examples.trans: There is something important I want to say.
There is no time right now.

meanings.note: Indefinite إشي مهم ('something important'); definite المهم ('the important thing / what matters is...').

examples.trans: I have an important matter to discuss.
What matters is that we be honest.

meanings.note: Form II khallas means 'finish something' (نخلصه), while Form I khalas min (أخلص من ظلمهم) means 'be rid of'.

examples.trans: I finished the homework early.
I'm going to put an end to the problem.

meanings.note: Placed before a noun for 'first' (أول مرة), or at the end of a clause adverbially for 'first / beforehand' (نخلصه أول).

examples.trans: This is the first time I see you here.
Let's finish homework first.

meanings.note: Used in questions like عن جد؟ or والله جد؟ ('oh really? / seriously?').

examples.trans: Are you being serious?
Honestly, I'm really happy for you.

meanings.note: Active participle of عرف, regularly used instead of the present tense for current awareness (إنتي عارفة منيح).

examples.trans: I know the whole story.
I didn't know about the appointment.

meanings.note: Clause-linking particle taking pronoun suffixes directly: إني ('that I'), إنك ('that you').

examples.trans: I know that you're honest.
I thought that I was late.

meanings.note: Takes a direct object suffix (أستأذنك) or من (بتستأذني مني) for asking someone's permission.

examples.trans: I have to ask the teacher's permission.
I asked permission before leaving.

meanings.note: Before an indefinite singular noun, كل means 'every' (كل يوم، كل إشي); with الـ (الكل) it means 'everyone'; with suffixes (كلنا، كلهم، كلها) 'all of us/them/it'.

examples.trans: Everyone knows the story.
We see each other every day.

meanings.note: Everyday casual 'yes' in Amman speech, softer and more informal than نعم.

examples.trans: Yeah, I'm coming with you.
Yeah, of course I know her.

meanings.note: Everyday time conjunction for both past ('when I went down': لما نزلت) and general/future events (لما الإشي يدخل بخطتي).

examples.trans: Call me when you arrive.
I was happy when I saw you.

meanings.note: Literally 'enter'; يدخل بخطتي means 'enters into / affects my plan'.

examples.trans: The teacher walked into the classroom.
Don't get into a matter that doesn't concern you.

meanings.note: With possessive endings, -ة becomes -ت-: خطتي ('my plan'), خطتك ('your plan'), خطتنا ('our plan').

examples.trans: We have a clear plan.
What do you think of our plan?

meanings.note: Core Levantine verb for 'come': past إجيت / إجت, b-present باجي / بتيجي.

examples.trans: Why didn't you come yesterday?
Next time I'll come with you.

meanings.note: Takes pronoun endings مني (from me), منها (of/from her), منكم (of you): تكون من شلتها ('be part of her clique'), بخاف منها ('afraid of her').

examples.trans: I got off the bus.
Which one of you saw what happened?

meanings.note: Used before nouns (قبل بوقت 'ahead of time'), before ما + verb (قبل ما تعصب 'before she gets angry'), or alone at the end of a clause ('beforehand').

examples.trans: I arrived at school before the bell.
Tell me before you go.

meanings.note: Said politely to say 'you're welcome', or sharply with rising intonation ('Excuse me?!') to challenge what someone just said.

examples.trans: Excuse me, what did you say?
Thank you! — You're welcome.

meanings.note: Spoken feminine singular 'you', spelled with final ي to reflect the Jordanian pronunciation inti.

examples.trans: Are you a new girl here?
What do you think?

meanings.note: With suffixes, acts as the Levantine reflexive ('myself/themselves': حالهم), 'alone' (لحالك), and 'one's own business' (خليكم بحالكم).

examples.trans: I studied the lesson by myself.
Leave me to myself, please.

meanings.note: Takes suffixes معي (with me), معك (with you), معها (with her), معنا (with us), معكم (with you all), معهم (with them), and forms مع السلامة! ('Goodbye!').

examples.trans: Come sit with us.
Goodbye, see you tomorrow!

meanings.note: After مع, مع بعض means 'together / with one another'.

examples.trans: We walk home together.
We studied together yesterday.

meanings.note: High-frequency Jordanian discourse word meaning 'okay, settled!' or 'drop it / enough!'.

examples.trans: Deal, we're agreed.
Enough, be quiet now.

meanings.note: Takes pronoun endings: علي (on/about me), عليكي (to you, f.), عليها (to her), علينا (on/for us), عليكم (on you, pl.). Often contracts to عـ before الـ.

examples.trans: Count on me in this matter.
They lied about me in front of the teacher.

meanings.note: Spoken Levantine counterpart of ظل; before another verb (يضل يتحمل، بتضلك تخططي) it means 'keep on doing'.

examples.trans: I stayed at school until afternoon.
You keep asking the same question.

meanings.note: Spoken Levantine form of يد. Idioms: بإيدي ('in my power/control') and إيد واحدة ('one hand' = united).

examples.trans: The matter wasn't in my hands.
We must stay united.

meanings.note: After a noun, means 'one' (إشي واحد، سؤال واحد، إيد واحدة); with الـ (الواحد) it is the everyday impersonal subject 'a person / one'.

examples.trans: A person has to tell the truth.
I have just one question.

meanings.note: Appears in everyday speech mainly in fixed polite phrases like إلى اللقاء! ('Until next time!').

examples.trans: Until next time, girls!
We reached the end of the lesson.

meanings.note: Used in the warm standard farewell إلى اللقاء! ('Until we meet again! / Until next time!').

examples.trans: Until next time soon!
It was a very nice meeting.
